observations: The function under consideration is real-valued and defined on all of the real line.
As x approaches 0, the quotient f(x)/x^2 is required to have a specified limiting behavior.
The question asks whether that limiting behavior alone guarantees a local differentiability property near 0.
The correct answer is negative, so the limiting behavior by itself does not guarantee that local differentiability property.
The setting involves six distinct positive integers, and the quantities under discussion are sums of unordered pairs of them.
No pair sum can equal 2, so every prime pair sum must be odd.
A pair sum is odd exactly when one integer in the pair is odd and the other is even.
If r of the six integers are odd, then the number of odd-even pairs is r(6-r), and this quantity is at most 9.
The problem concerns trailing zeros of a factorial N! when it is written in a prime base p.
For a prime p, the number of trailing zeros of N! in base p equals v_p(N!), the exponent of p in the prime factorization of N!.
Legendre's formula gives v_p(N!) as floor(N/p) + floor(N/p^2) + floor(N/p^3) + ... .
The desired prime is the least prime p for which v_p(N!) is strictly less than p.
There are three distinct volunteers, and each receives a positive integer number of indivisible marbles.
The three assigned counts form an ordered triple (a,b,c) of positive integers whose sum is a fixed total T.
Lewis can steal from all three exactly when some integer n > 1 divides each of a,b,c, which is equivalent to gcd(a,b,c) > 1.
The desired distributions are those ordered triples for which no n > 1 divides all three counts; the final task asks for their number.
The unknown is an odd integer denoted by k.
The expression to be evaluated is (k^2 - 1)/8.
Substituting k=2n+1 for an integer n simplifies that expression to n(n+1)/2.
The quantity n(n+1)/2 is the nth triangular number, so the expression is triangular whenever k is odd.
The object under consideration is a linear map between real normed vector spaces, with its domain and codomain dimensions left unspecified.
A hypothesis is imposed on the quotient of the norm of the image and the norm of the input as the input approaches the zero vector.
The desired conclusion is that the map is identically zero, meaning it sends every vector in its domain to the zero vector.
If the map is not identically zero, then there is a nonzero vector v with L(v) not equal to 0, and along h = t v the quotient ||L(h)||/||h|| equals ||L(v)||/||v|| for every t > 0.
The problem asks for real values of a single variable x that satisfy an equation involving square roots.
The equation has the form sqrt(A)+sqrt(B)=sqrt(C)+sqrt(D), where A, B, C, and D are quadratic expressions in x.
The four quadratic radicands can be paired so that the difference in each pair is the same linear expression in x.
For any real solution, all four radicands must be nonnegative.
The problem concerns a sequence h_n indexed by positive integers.
The sequence satisfies a first-order linear recurrence with a constant forcing term.
The initial condition is chosen so that extending the sequence by h_0=0 makes the recurrence valid at n=1.
The requested formula is to be found from the ordinary generating function H(x)=sum h_n x^n.
The variable x is real and lies strictly between 0 and 1.
On this interval, the product x(1-x) is positive and never exceeds 1/4.
The infinite series is formed by taking successive powers of the single quantity x(1-x).
Because x(1-x) is between 0 and 1, the series is geometric and can be summed by the geometric-series formula.
The discussion takes place in a metric space with its metric topology.
A base for the topology is a family of open sets such that every open set is a union of members of the family.
The question asks whether a countable subset of the space can always be found with a specified topological role.
The final answer to that yes-or-no question is affirmative.
The problem concerns the rank of a 2-by-3 matrix whose entries are affine expressions in three variables.
Since the matrix has only two rows, its rank is at most 2, so the only possible exact ranks are 0, 1, or 2.
The requested result is the exact rank of that matrix under two polynomial constraints on the variables.
To prove the rank is 2, it is enough to find one nonzero 2-by-2 minor.
Let B = {v_i}_{i=1}^n be a finite basis of a vector space V.
Let T: V -> V be a linear operator, and let A = [T]_B be its matrix in the basis B.
The first column of A is the coordinate vector of T(v_1) in the basis B.
The requested quantity is the sum of all entries of the matrix [T^{-1}]_B, which is A^{-1}.
The original problem asks for the number of integer-coordinate points on a hyperbola of the form x^2 - y^2 = C, where C is a positive integer constant.
For any such point, the quantities u = x - y and v = x + y are integers whose product is C.
The inverse relations x = (u + v)/2 and y = (v - u)/2 show that u and v must have the same parity.
In the intended case, C is even, so u and v cannot both be odd; therefore any valid pair must have u and v both even.
The modulus is an odd prime p.
The multiplicative group modulo p is cyclic.
The objects being counted are primitive roots modulo p, represented by residues from 1 to p.
Counting primitive roots is the same as counting generators of that cyclic group.
The requested result is a count of ordered triples of natural numbers.
The three entries are constrained simultaneously by their greatest common divisor and their least common multiple.
The greatest common divisor is fixed as 15, so its prime factorization is 3^1 times 5^1.
The least common multiple is fixed and uses only the primes 3 and 5, with the exponent of 5 larger than the exponent of 3.
The sequence is indexed by integers n≥2, and each term x_n is defined as an nth root of a positive expression.
Inside that root, 1 is added to a finite sum whose index runs from k=2 to n.
The summands are (k-1)(k-1)!, which can be rewritten as k!-(k-1)!.
Because the sum telescopes, the expression under the nth root simplifies to n!, so x_n=(n!)^{1/n}.
The function f is allowed to be any polynomial of degree at most 2.
For every such f, a definite integral of f over the fixed interval [0,2] equals f(alpha)+f(beta).
The numbers alpha and beta are fixed unknowns that make this equality true for all allowed f.
The requested result is a constant multiple of (alpha-beta)^2, but the multiplier is not stated in these observations.
There is a finite family of sets, and all sets in the family have the same finite size.
Each set in the family contains exactly 45 elements.
The union of any two distinct sets contains exactly 89 elements.
The requested quantity is the number of elements in the union of all sets in the family.
The source asks whether an infinite sequence of natural numbers can be chosen.
The condition concerns every finite partial sum of that sequence.
A perfect power means a number of the form m^k with integer k at least 2.
It is enough to make every partial sum congruent to 2 modulo 4.
The problem asks for the value of a definite integral.
The integrand is 1/(x+sqrt(1-x^2)).
The lower limit of integration is 0.
The upper limit is a positive number in the domain of the integrand, but its exact value is not stated in these clues.
The unknowns form an ordered triple of real numbers, and the equations are invariant under the cyclic shift (x,y,z) -> (y,z,x).
Each equation mixes one variable with the square of the next variable and the fourth power of the remaining variable, all summing to zero.
Every coordinate of any solution is forced to be nonpositive.
Writing x=-a, y=-b, z=-c with a,b,c >= 0 turns the system into a=b^2+c^4 and its two cyclic rotations.
The function depends on a positive parameter a and on a real variable x restricted to x>0.
The question concerns the behavior of this function as x approaches 0 from the right, specifically whether it is unbounded in every right neighborhood of 0.
The function contains oscillatory factors involving 1/x^a and x^{-a}, so the parameter a controls both the frequency and the power of x.
The requested result is a set of values of a, not a numerical value of the function or a single parameter.
The sequence starts at 0 and all of its terms are non-negative integers.
At each step, the next term is either 0 or the previous term increased by 1 and then reduced modulo a fixed positive modulus.
The sequence stops as soon as the value one less than that modulus has appeared for the second time.
The quantity to be counted is the number of such sequences with a prescribed total number of zeros, and the requested result is that count modulo the same modulus.
The task concerns a line integral of a vector field along a closed curve in three-dimensional space.
The intended evaluation uses the curl theorem, so the line integral is converted to a surface integral of the curl over a surface bounded by the curve.
The vector field has a first component involving a linear y term and a sine of x, a second component involving z squared and a cosine of y, and a third component that is cubic in x.
The curve is parametrized by x=sin t, y=cos t, and z equal to some multiple of sin 2t, with t running through one full period.
Let omega and z be complex numbers with |omega|=1.
Define theta as the argument of (omega - z)/z.
Set u=(omega-z)/z; then u+1=omega/z, so |u+1|=1/|z|.
Thus theta is the argument of a point u on the circle centered at -1 with radius 1/|z|.
A positive constant a is used as a scale in the expression being integrated.
The object under study is a limit of integrals over the nonnegative half-line [0,∞).
A parameter n tends to infinity, and the integrand depends on n through a power of the scaled variable.
The integrand is bounded between 0 and 1, and the requested limit is a single number depending on a.
There are three nonnegative real variables, say x, y, and z.
The variables satisfy the single linear constraint x + y + z = 3.
Each variable is restricted to the same closed interval [0, a], where the exact upper endpoint a is not supplied in these observations.
The quantity to be maximized is x^3 + y^3 + z^3.
The limit is taken as n tends to infinity, with n understood as a positive integer.
The expression is a product of two factors: one is n times a natural logarithm of 1 minus 1/n.
The other factor is a cosine whose argument is π times the square root of a quadratic expression in n.
The quadratic inside the square root has leading term 4n^2, so the square root is asymptotically 2n.
The problem concerns a limit as x approaches 0 of a quotient whose numerator is the sine of a nested integral and whose denominator is x^8.
The outer integral is with respect to t from x^3 to x^2, and its integrand is an inner integral from 0 to t of g(s^2) with respect to s.
The function g is differentiable near 0 and satisfies g(0)=0, so only its local first-order behavior near 0 should affect the leading term.
Because the nested integral vanishes as x approaches 0, the sine factor is asymptotically equivalent to that nested integral.
The motion takes place on the integer lattice, so each jump displacement has two integer coordinate components.
The j-th jump has length j, so its squared length equals j^2.
Returning to the starting point means the total horizontal displacement and the total vertical displacement are both zero.
Modulo 2, an odd-length jump forces exactly one coordinate component to be odd, while an even-length jump forces both coordinate components to be even.
There are 160 initial sets \(A_1,\ldots,A_{160}\), and each has a distinct positive integer size.
In each step \(k\), one chooses some of the initial sets and removes the same positive number \(c_k\) of elements from every chosen set; the removed elements form a new set \(M_k\).
The procedure continues until every element of every initial set \(A_i\) has been removed.
For each \(i\), if \(S_i\) is the set of steps in which \(A_i\) is chosen, then \(\sum_{k\in S_i} c_k=|A_i|\).
A prime number p is the main parameter in the original problem.
The central expression is a binomial coefficient whose lower entry is p.
The upper entry of that binomial coefficient is p^2+1.
The original question asks whether a certain divisibility statement about this binomial coefficient holds for every such prime p.
The words are strings whose symbols are chosen from the seven digits 0,1,2,3,4,5,6.
In any valid word, each pair of neighboring digits must differ by exactly 1.
The quantity to be found is the remainder of the number of valid words of a fixed positive length after division by a positive integer.
For a fixed length, the count can be tracked by the last digit, because the next digit is forced to be one less or one greater when possible.
Each integer n can be written as s^2 m with m squarefree, so sqrt n = s sqrt m.
Terms with the same squarefree part m combine into a single coefficient times sqrt m.
The squarefree part 1 contributes only an integer constant and does not require a square-root term.
For m>1 squarefree, the coefficient from the sum is positive because n=m itself contributes, so each such m must appear as a nonzero radical term.
The function f is assumed to be Riemann integrable on a closed bounded interval [a,b].
A hypothesis is imposed on integrals of products f g over [a,b] for a class of test functions g.
The test functions g in that hypothesis are continuous on [a,b].
The final answer is affirmative for a pointwise conclusion about the values of f at its continuity points.
For each positive integer n, S_n denotes the sum 1^3+2^3+...+n^3.
The sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the triangular number T_n=n(n+1)/2.
If T_n has prime factorization ∏ p_i^{a_i}, then the divisor count of S_n is ∏(2a_i+1).
Therefore every attainable divisor count τ(S_n) is odd, so even candidate values of m cannot occur.
The number x is positive and rational.
The number x is not an integer.
The expression under consideration is x raised to the power x.
If x^x is written as a quotient of positive integers, the question concerns a divisibility property of that quotient's numerator and denominator.
The game uses a finite set of distinct cards, and a complete combination is a designated 3-card subset.
Each card belongs to exactly four designated combinations.
Let N be the total number of cards; the value of N is not given in these clues.
The requested quantity is the smallest opening-hand size that guarantees at least one complete combination.
A family is made from 3-element subsets of a finite ground set.
Any two distinct members of the family share at most one element.
The problem asks for the maximum possible number of members in such a family.
Each member contains exactly 3 unordered pairs, and the intersection condition prevents any unordered pair from appearing in two different members.
A sequence begins with a_1=1 and a_2=2.
For n>=2, the first difference d_n=a_n-a_{n-1} satisfies d_{n+1}=((n-1)/(n+1))d_n.
This implies d_n=2/[n(n-1)] for n>=2, so the sequence can be summed by telescoping.
The resulting closed form is a_n=3-2/n, which increases toward 3 from below.
The parameter a is positive.
One curve is an exponential y=e^{kx} for some positive constant k, and the other is the upward-opening parabola y=a x^2.
A common tangent is a straight line that is tangent to both curves.
The target is the set of a-values for which exactly two common tangents occur.
The problem concerns a definite integral over the positive half-line, from 0 to infinity.
Its integrand is the reciprocal of a product of two positive factors, one of which is quadratic in x.
The other factor involves x raised to a positive parameter, and the value is independent of that parameter.
A reciprocal substitution x=1/t is the natural symmetry to exploit.
The Taylor series is taken about the origin for a complex function that is a constant multiple of tan z divided by a rational factor.
The radius of convergence is the distance from 0 to the nearest singularity of that complex function.
The rational factor has a denominator of the form 1 + a z^2 with a positive real parameter, so it contributes purely imaginary poles.
At those imaginary poles, tan z is finite and nonzero, so they are genuine poles rather than removable singularities.
The two curves are graphs of the same cubic function, with the second graph obtained by a horizontal translation of the first by a nonzero parameter.
The condition that the curves meet in exactly two points translates into a quadratic equation in the intersection x-coordinate having two distinct real roots.
The bounded region is the area between the two curves over the interval between those two intersection x-coordinates.
The problem asks for the largest possible value of this bounded area as the translation parameter varies over all admissible values.
A positive integer x is used as the base of a large power in the dividend.
The divisor is the quadratic x^2+x+1.
The dividend has the form x^n - x for some positive integer exponent n.
The requested result is the least nonnegative remainder of that dividend modulo the divisor.
A repunit R_n is the n-digit number 111...1, equivalently R_n = (10^n - 1)/9.
The original question asks whether a fixed prime can be the least prime divisor of some repunit.
The final answer to that question is negative.
For a prime p not equal to 3, p divides R_n is equivalent to 10^n ≡ 1 mod p, since 9 is invertible modulo p.
The function f is defined on the interval [0, π] and has a continuous second derivative there.
The problem considers the integral from 0 to π of [f(x)+f''(x)] sin x dx.
The endpoint value f(π) is specified to be 1.
The quantity to be determined is the endpoint value f(0).

The integer n is negative and has four digits, so it lies between -9999 and -1000 inclusive.
The integer n is congruent to 1 modulo some positive integer m.
The requested value is the greatest integer satisfying the four-digit negative and congruence conditions.
Two sequences {a_n} and {b_n} are involved, and {b_n} is obtained from {a_n} by a rule that alternates between selecting an a-term and taking a square root of an a-term.
For odd n, b_n is an a-term whose index is (n+1)/2; for even n, b_n is the square root of a later a-term.
The sequence {b_n} is geometric, so it has a common ratio r and can be written as b_n = b_1 r^{n-1}.
The target is the general term formula for {a_n}, and the data include a positive numerical condition involving a_2 and b_2.
The original problem asks for all integer solutions of a single congruence modulo 2016.
The modulus factors as 2^5 * 3^2 * 7, so the congruence can be studied modulo 32, 9, and 7.
The right-hand side of the congruence is the integer 5.

The quantity under consideration is the sum ab/c + bc/a + ca/b.
The variables are constrained by a symmetric quadratic condition a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = N, where N is a fixed positive constant not given in the clues.

The lowest exponent in the base sum is 3, so the fourth power has a common factor x^12.
After removing that common factor, the requested coefficient becomes a coefficient of a positive power in (1+x+...+x^m)^4 for some positive integer m.
Such a coefficient counts ordered quadruples of nonnegative integers with a common upper bound m and a fixed total.
